meeting_header: Date: 2027-05-20 | Time: 14:00-15:15 PDT | Duration: 75 minutes | Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Crestline CTO), Rajiv Menon (Head of Infra), Elena Torres (Security)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll kick off w- uh, overview then go deep into artifacts and drivers. We're planning to cover artifact delivery, offline licensing, and some runtime perf knobs.
[00:00:22] Miguel: Hi Laura, Rajiv, Elena, nice to meet you. I'm Miguel, I'll go through the install pieces and then we can dive into KV cache and batching trade-offs.
[00:00:35] Laura: Thanks, Miguel, hey Samira. Quick note, we're regulated so air-gap is must, and our infra team will handle transfers, so we need checksums and a deterministic install path.
[00:00:48] Rajiv: Yep, also need offline driver licensing for the GPUs, procurement needs serial- or entitlement-based keys. We can't do any outbound calls from the cluster during install.
[00:01:02] Elena: From security side, we need signed artifacts, the hash, SLSA-like provenance if possible, and an inventory of binaries.
[00:01:15] Samira: Absolutely, we'll provide signed packages and checksums. Miguel, can you walk through the artifact types?
[00:01:25] Miguel: Sure. For air-gapped installs we provide: container images as tarballs (OCI), a tar.gz containing RPMs/debs for the control-plane components, and a driver bundle for NVIDIA -- that's the trickiest. The typical delivery is: artifact bundle (redwood-private-vX.tar.gz), a drivers package (nvidia-drivers-offline.tar.gz), and an offline-license file that your ops will apply with our activation tool. We'll include MD5 and SHA256 and a small installer script.
[00:01:57] Laura: Are the containers built against containerd or docker? We run containerd in prod.
[00:02:03] Miguel: Containerd, yes. We test both but our tarballs use OCI images that containerd load can accept. We'll include guidance for ctr or nerdctl load commands.
[00:02:15] Rajiv: For the GPU drivers, do you require a specific NVIDIA driver version? We run A100s, driver set is 525.X in our infra.
[00:02:24] Miguel: We recommend >= 525 for CUDA 12 compatibility; for A100 we usually target the 525 or 535 trees depending on CUDA and cuDNN. We'll provide a manifest that maps recommended driver versions to supported model runtimes. If you have vendor-locked builds, we can test against your exact driver if you can provide the .run or rpms.
[00:02:46] Elena: How does the offline license activation work, is it a phone-home or can it be fully offline?
[00:02:53] Samira: It's fully offline. We supply an activation token file and an encrypt-signed license blob. The installer accepts a license file and a local activation command that validates signatures locally. No outbound network call is required. We'll also supply a step to generate a host fingerprint for your records.
[00:03:12] Miguel: Important note: the NVIDIA driver itself is licensed by NVIDIA, so you'll need to have the appropriate entitlements. Our bundle contains the driver binaries but distribution rights depend on your agreement; we can provide an instruction doc to get offline-licensed driver packages from NVIDIA if required.
[00:03:32] Rajiv: OK, procurement will handle entitlements. For the installer, what user privileges are required? We prefer non-root where possible.
[00:03:40] Miguel: Driver install requires root for kernel modules. The Redwood runtime and control plane can run under non-root containers, but the initial driver install and nvidia-modprobe steps need elevated privileges. We'll document the minimal sudo steps.
[00:03:55] [00:04:02] Speaker 2: (inaudible) ... and also storage for KV cache should be on fast NVMe?
[00:04:08] Miguel: Good point. For KV cache and large sequence lengths, NVMe is strongly recommended. Our runtime keeps KV cache in GPU VRAM primarily, but we spill or checkpoint to local NVMe for long context persistence depending on config. We'll discuss sizing in the perf section.
[00:04:28] Samira: Let's pivot to runtime perf. Miguel, can you talk about batching and latency/throughput trade-offs?
[00:04:36] Miguel: Sure. Redwood's serving runtime supports dynamic batching and continuous batching modes. For low p95 latency (target you mentioned 150ms) you want small batch sizes and concurrency. For throughput-focused workloads we suggest larger batches, e.g., batch size 8-32 depending on sequence length. There's an interplay with KV cache: if you have effective prefix caching, you reduce compute per request so larger batch sizes are feasible without blowing latency.
[00:05:04] Rajiv: Our expected request pattern is chatty — many short requests with repeated context. We care about p95 under 200ms.
[00:05:11] Miguel: With chatty short requests, prefix KV cache helps a lot. If the conversation has repeated prefixes we can do prefix caching at the serving layer and skip recomputing those tokens. That reduces end-to-end token compute. For sequence length ~512 and batch size 4-8, in fp16 on A100 we typically see token latencies around 25-40ms per token, but end-to-end depends on prompt prep and reranking.
[00:05:39] Elena: You mentioned fp16, what about quantization? Security/quality team wants deterministic outputs. Are 4-bit quant models deterministic?
[00:05:48] Miguel: Quantization is a trade-off. 8-bit quant (INT8 or simulated) often retains very high fidelity and is deterministic for a given kernel, but 4-bit (e.g., int4) can introduce small quality variance — and some implementations rely on stochastic rounding. For regulated use we usually recommend fp16 or 8-bit quant where you can do validation against your eval prompts. We provide quant profiles and regression tests so you can measure deviation.
[00:06:13] Samira: Also note we can supply model variants — quantized and fp16 — and you can pin rollout policies per route so sensitive routes use fp16.
[00:06:22] Laura: For our POC we want throughput of ~200 reqs/min with 512 seq and p95 <200ms. Is that realistic on a single A100?
[00:06:31] Miguel: It's borderline for single GPU depending on model size. For a 13B class model with kv-caching and batching tuned, a single A100 might achieve that if you keep batch sizes optimized and have heavy prefix cache hit rates. For larger 70B models you'll need multiple GPUs or model parallelism. We'll put concrete numbers in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[00:06:51] Rajiv: Model parallelism is... we don't want extra complexity. If we go multi-GPU, does Redwood manage sharding and runtime?
[00:06:58] Miguel: Yes, our runtime supports sharded execution and we handle KV cache sharding and coherence. But in air-gapped installs you need to ensure low-latency interconnect (Infiniband) and correct RDMA drivers. We'll include driver versions and kernel params for that.
[00:07:15] Elena: What about security around the KV cache — is anything persisted unencrypted?
[00:07:21] Miguel: By default KV cache in GPU memory is ephemeral and not written to disk. For checkpointing/spill to NVMe we support encrypted local volumes and integration with your KMS/HSM for key material. All on-disk artifacts can be encrypted and we provide instructions for LUKS or filesystem-level encryption.
[00:07:40] Laura: Can you walk us through what the offline install looks like step-by-step?
[00:07:45] Miguel: High-level: 1) Ops copies our artifact tarball to a bastion node, verifies MD5/SHA256 and signature, 2) Extract and load OCI images into containerd, 3) Install NVIDIA driver rpms or run installer (root), 4) Load offline license file via our activation CLI which writes a signed blob to /var/lib/redwood/license, 5) Start the control-plane containers and do a local smoke test which hits runtime endpoints and validates GPU visibility and KV cache warm-up. We'll include exact CLI snippets in the runbook.
[00:08:18] Rajiv: For smoke tests, what do you check? GPU visibility, health endpoints, and a quick gen?
[00:08:24] Miguel: Exactly — nvidia-smi, runtime /health, a small model forward to validate kernels and quant behavior, and a KV cache sanity check. We also run a short micro-benchmark that measures tokens/s at a few seq lengths.
[00:08:36] [00:08:44] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) ... how do you handle kernel selection?
[00:08:47] Miguel: Kernel selection is automatic: runtime profiles model and sequence distribution and picks optimized kernels. We ship a set of kernels optimized for different driver/CUDA combos. In air-gapped installs we include the kernel libs for the recommended driver versions. If you bump kernel/driver versions we'll need to rebuild or re-profile.
[00:09:07] Laura: Is there any manual tuning we should expect post-install?
[00:09:11] Miguel: Usually yes. We often tune batching windows, max queue latency, and cache sizes based on real traffic. We'll recommend initial defaults and then run a short tuning phase during the POC where we collect latency and cost numbers and tune batching thresholds.
[00:09:27] Elena: One more question on provenance: can you provide signatures for each OCI image layer?
[00:09:32] Samira: We can provide cosign signatures for images and a signed manifest. We'll attach a provenance bundle to the artifact.
[00:09:40] Rajiv: Regarding driver entitlements, how do we prove we can distribute the driver?
[00:09:45] Miguel: We'll provide guidance; if your NVIDIA contract allows offline distribution you can use the rpms we include. If not, we provide an instruction doc for you to request the offline driver tarball directly from NVIDIA and a small patch to our installer to point to a local path.
[00:09:59] Laura: For the POC timeline, we want to start install next week and have a perf report by end of next week. Is that doable?
[00:10:06] Samira: Yes, if procurement can confirm driver entitlements and you can accept the artifact transfer week of 24th, we can schedule an install and a 2-3 day tuning window, delivering a perf report within 5 business days.
[00:10:18] Miguel: I'll also include microbenchmark configs: seq lengths 128/512/1024, batch sizes 1/4/8/16, and both fp16 and int8 quant profiles so you can compare.
[00:10:29] Elena: For monitoring and logs in air-gapped mode, do you push telemetry out?
[00:10:33] Miguel: No outbound by default. We ship a local observability stack that persists metrics and traces to on-prem storage. If you opt-in to a hybrid model we can export aggregated metrics via secure egress, but for pure air-gap everything stays local.
[00:10:48] Samira: Quick note on support: for dedicated installs we provide a support entitlement and we can arrange remote debug sessions via pre-approved bastion access, or on-site if needed.
[00:10:58] Rajiv: Good. Anything else on quantization and model variants?
[00:11:02] Miguel: One thing: when you quantize, especially to 4-bit, mismatch in tokenization or subtle pre/post processing can show drift. We'll run your eval prompt set across fp16 and quant versions and provide delta metrics so you can decide which routes get which model.
[00:11:19] Laura: That sounds good. One operational question: how are updates handled? We don't want to do full reinstall each patch.
[00:11:26] Miguel: We support delta updates for our control plane and runtime. For driver updates you do need the driver install step, which is more heavyweight. We'll provide an update bundle and a dry-run mode to validate.
[00:11:40] Samira: Alright, let's recap next steps. We'll send the artifact bundle and checksums, Miguel will send the runbook and benchmark configs, and we'll schedule the install window. Rajiv will confirm driver entitlements. Elena will share the list of required signed artifacts for security review.
[00:11:57] Laura: Confirming we want install week of May 24th and perf report by May 28th.
[00:12:04] Samira: Got it. We'll target that. Thanks all.
[00:12:10] Miguel: Thanks, everyone. We'll follow up with the links and runbook.
[00:12:14] [END OF RECORDING]
